Malicious URL Detection — Step 2: Model Training, Comparison, Tuning and Evaluation¶

Input: the Step 1 outputs: data/processed/{train,val,test}.parquet (43 features, order fixed by feature_list.json), the fitted models/feature_extractor.joblib, and the domain-grouped split.

Rules used throughout

  • Same 43 features, same splits, random_state=42 everywhere.
  • Every cross-validation uses grouped folds (by registered domain) from src/data.py, passed as an explicit list of splits, so a website never appears in both the training and the scoring part of a fold.
  • The test set is used once, at the very end, only for the selected model and the tuned RF.
  • Every fitted model, its predictions and its timings are cached in models/cache/. Re-running this notebook reuses the real training run instead of retraining.

Time plan. The benchmark above was run before any training (scripts/step2_benchmark.py). Compute is not the bottleneck: a full-train RF(200) takes ~16 s. Memory is. One full-depth RF(200) on 591k rows needs ~2.2 GB of RAM and an ExtraTrees(200) ~4.7 GB, while only ~4.7 GB was free. Therefore:

  • big models are trained one at a time, evaluated while in memory, saved (compressed) and freed;
  • the RF search runs a memory guard first (section 5). It estimates the worst combination in the search space on one CV fold, multiplies by the number of workers, and lowers n_jobs (never the search space) until this fits in free RAM minus 1 GB. That way nothing pages to disk.

Two extra test sets (never used for training or tuning)¶

  • OpenPhish snapshot (data/external/openphish_feed_2026-11-24.txt): live phishing URLs collected after our datasets. These are all malicious, so the metric is recall.
  • Real-world benign set (data/external/realworld_benign_urls.csv): 86 popular legitimate URLs written exactly as Chrome sends them, including Google search, Indian banks and government sites, and legitimate login pages. They are all benign, so the metric is the number of false positives. It was committed before any model was trained (commit 558b426), so it cannot be cherry-picked.

None of them is an exact copy of a URL in our data, but 248 sit on registered domains we already have, almost all free-hosting platforms: pages.dev alone has 187 URLs, then vercel.app (13), weebly.com (11) and github.io (7). Only 50 URLs are on never-seen domains, and those are the real test of generalisation. The real-world benign set has 86 URLs in 17 categories.

2. Problem type & algorithm choice¶

Why classification. Each URL gets one of two known labels: 0 = benign, 1 = malicious. We have 856k labelled examples, so this is supervised binary classification. The model outputs a probability P(malicious), and a threshold turns it into a decision. Section 9 picks that threshold so that false alarms on normal browsing stay at or below 1%.

Why these 13 models. They cover the main families, from simple to complex:

family models what it tests
single (linear / distance / probabilistic / one tree) Logistic Regression, KNN, Gaussian Naive Bayes, Decision Tree how far a simple model gets; LR/KNN need scaled features (StandardScaler in a Pipeline)
bagging Random Forest, Extra Trees, Bagging(DT) many deep trees trained on random variations of the data, then averaged
boosting AdaBoost, HistGradientBoosting, XGBoost, LightGBM trees trained one after another, each fixing the previous errors
combination Soft Voting, Stacking (RF + XGB + LGBM) combining different strong models

Ensemble learning in one paragraph each

  • Bagging ("bootstrap aggregating"). Train many trees, each on a random resample of the rows (Random Forest also uses a random subset of features at every split). Then average their votes. One deep tree memorises noise; the average of 200 different trees cancels much of it, which lowers variance.
  • Boosting. Train small trees in sequence, where every new tree focuses on the URLs the current ensemble still gets wrong (AdaBoost re-weights them; gradient boosting fits the remaining error). This lowers bias step by step.
  • Voting. Ask several different models and average their probabilities (soft voting). If they make different mistakes, the average makes fewer.
  • Stacking. Like voting, but a small "meta-model" (here Logistic Regression) learns how much to trust each model. It learns from out-of-fold predictions, so it never sees a model's prediction on that model's own training rows.

3. Baseline comparison: 13 models¶

All models use the same 43 features and the full training split (591k rows), with one exception: KNN is trained on a 100k grouped, class-stratified sample, because it stores the whole training set and compares every query against it. KNN is still evaluated on the full validation set. Training F1 is measured on the same 100k grouped training sample for every model, to show the overfitting gap.

Latency = one URL, including feature extraction, on one CPU thread (median of 200 calls), like a small Render instance. Size = joblib.dump(model, compress=3).

def rf200(**kw):
    return RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=200, n_jobs=-1, random_state=RS, **kw)

def xgb_default():
    return XGBClassifier(tree_method="hist", n_estimators=400, learning_rate=0.1, max_depth=8,
                         n_jobs=-1, random_state=RS, eval_metric="logloss")

def lgbm_default():
    return LGBMClassifier(n_estimators=400, learning_rate=0.05, num_leaves=63, n_jobs=-1,
                          random_state=RS, verbose=-1)

def dt_extra(e):
    return {"depth": int(e.get_depth()), "n_leaves": int(e.get_n_leaves())}

BASELINES = [  # key, label, family, factory, rows
    ("logreg", "Logistic Regression", "single",
     lambda: make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000, random_state=RS)), "full"),
    ("decision_tree", "Decision Tree", "single", lambda: DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=RS), "full"),
    ("knn", "KNN (k=5, 100k)", "single",
     lambda: make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), KNeighborsClassifier(n_jobs=-1)), "100k"),
    ("naive_bayes", "Gaussian Naive Bayes", "single", GaussianNB, "full"),
    ("random_forest", "Random Forest", "bagging", rf200, "full"),
    ("extra_trees", "Extra Trees", "bagging",
     lambda: ExtraTreesClassifier(n_estimators=200, n_jobs=-1, random_state=RS), "full"),
    ("bagging", "Bagging (DT x50)", "bagging",
     lambda: BaggingClassifier(DecisionTreeClassifier(), n_estimators=50, n_jobs=-1, random_state=RS), "full"),
    ("adaboost", "AdaBoost (stumps)", "boosting", lambda: AdaBoostClassifier(n_estimators=200, random_state=RS), "full"),
    ("hist_gb", "HistGradientBoosting", "boosting", lambda: HistGradientBoostingClassifier(random_state=RS), "full"),
    ("xgboost", "XGBoost", "boosting", xgb_default, "full"),
    ("lightgbm", "LightGBM", "boosting", lgbm_default, "full"),
]
LABELS = {k: lab for k, lab, *_ in BASELINES}
LABELS.update({"voting": "Soft Voting (RF+XGB+LGBM)", "stacking": "Stacking (RF+XGB+LGBM)"})

t_all = time.perf_counter()
for key, lab, fam, fac, rows in BASELINES:

# 12 Soft Voting: averages the probabilities of the already-trained RF, XGB and LGBM (no refit)
if not store.has("voting"):
    names = ["random_forest", "xgboost", "lightgbm"]
    vote = M.SoftVotingPrefit([store.load(n) for n in names], names)
    store.ensure("voting", "combination", None, None, None, fitted=vote,
                 fit_time_s=sum(store.meta(n)["fit_time_s"] for n in names),
                 note="members reused; fit time = sum of member fit times")
    del vote; gc.collect()

# 13 Stacking: LR meta-model on out-of-fold probabilities from 3 GROUPED folds
def make_stack(rf, b1, b2):
    return StackingClassifier(estimators=[("rf", rf), ("xgb", b1), ("lgbm", b2)],
                              final_estimator=LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000, random_state=RS),
                              cv=cv3_full, stack_method="predict_proba", n_jobs=1)

def drop_cv(est):          # the explicit fold indices are not needed after fitting (saves ~14 MB)
    est.cv = 3

t0 = time.perf_counter()
m = store.ensure("stacking", "combination", lambda: make_stack(rf200(), xgb_default(), lgbm_default()),
                 Xtr, ytr, post_fit=drop_cv)
print(f"stacking fit {m['fit_time_s']:.0f}s, size {m['size_mb']:.1f} MB (cell {time.perf_counter() - t0:.0f}s)")
for k in ("voting", "stacking"):
    print(k, {x: store.meta(k)[x] for x in ("fit_time_s", "size_mb", "latency_ms_median")})

def model_row(key, label=None, thr=0.5):
    meta = store.meta(key)
    p = store.proba(key, "val")
    met = M.binary_metrics(yva, p, thr)
    f1_tr = f1_score(ytr[idx100k], store.proba(key, "train100k") >= thr)
    return {"model": label or LABELS.get(key, key), "key": key, "family": meta["family"], **met,
            "train_f1_100k": f1_tr, "f1_gap": f1_tr - met["f1"], "fit_time_s": meta["fit_time_s"],
            "latency_ms": meta["latency_ms_median"], "throughput_url_s": meta["throughput_urls_per_s"],
            "size_mb": meta["size_mb"]}

BASE_KEYS = [k for k, *_ in BASELINES] + ["voting", "stacking"]
comp = pd.DataFrame([model_row(k) for k in BASE_KEYS]).set_index("model").sort_values("f1", ascending=False)
M.save_metrics_table(comp, "baseline_comparison")
fmt = {c: "{:.4f}" for c in ["accuracy", "precision", "recall", "f1", "roc_auc", "pr_auc", "fpr", "train_f1_100k", "f1_gap"]}
fmt.update({"fit_time_s": "{:.1f}", "latency_ms": "{:.2f}", "throughput_url_s": "{:,.0f}", "size_mb": "{:,.2f}"})
display(comp.drop(columns="key").style.format(fmt))
dt = store.meta("decision_tree")
print(f"Decision Tree: depth {dt['depth']}, {dt['n_leaves']:,} leaves")
print("KNN: trained on the 100k grouped sample, evaluated on the FULL validation set")

Decision Tree: depth 54, 61,436 leaves
KNN: trained on the 100k grouped sample, evaluated on the FULL validation set

Insight: All 13 models were evaluated on the same 132,498 validation URLs from websites never seen in training.

  • Best: Stacking (F1 0.7425) and Soft Voting (0.7406), with XGBoost close behind (0.7379) at a fraction of the size. Random Forest reaches 0.7324.
  • Single models are clearly weaker: Logistic Regression 0.6424, Decision Tree 0.6391 (depth 54, 61,436 leaves), KNN 0.6657 and Naive Bayes 0.4953.

These scores are much lower than the ~0.97 often reported for this Kaggle data. Those results usually come from random splits that leak websites between train and test, and from the scheme/www shortcuts we removed in Step 1. Ours measure what the extension faces: new websites, URL text only. At the default 0.5 threshold every model still flags 7–22% of benign URLs, which is why section 9 tunes the threshold.

fig.tight_layout(rect=(0, 0, 1, 0.96)); V.savefig(fig, 14, "baseline_f1_rocauc_by_family"); plt.show()

Insight: The ensembles (Stacking, Voting, the boosters and RF) cluster at F1 0.72–0.74 and ROC-AUC 0.87–0.89. That is clearly above the single models (F1 ≤ 0.67) and AdaBoost (0.6065). Boosting has the best ROC-AUC per model (XGBoost 0.8859, LightGBM 0.8850), and combining RF with the boosters adds a little more (Voting 0.8908).

Insight: The bars show overfitting. Fully grown trees memorise the training URLs: Decision Tree train F1 0.965 vs validation 0.639 (gap 0.326), Bagging gap 0.255, Random Forest 0.233, Extra Trees 0.235. The boosters overfit much less (XGBoost 0.112, LightGBM 0.086, HistGB 0.045), and Logistic Regression hardly at all (0.025). Averaging trees (bagging) reduces the damage but does not remove it; limiting tree size does (see the tuned RF in section 5).

Insight: Size and latency separate the families much more than F1 does. The full-depth forests are 388 MB (RF), 836 MB (Extra Trees) and 69 MB (Bagging) compressed, and Voting/Stacking with the default RF are 391 MB, all far above the 25 MB limit. The boosters reach the same F1 at 0.17–1.6 MB and 1–5 ms per URL. On one thread, Stacking (22.5 ms) exceeds the 20 ms limit, and Voting (18.6 ms) is close to it.

4. Class weight: balanced vs none¶

The training data is 64% benign / 36% malicious. class_weight="balanced" gives each malicious URL more weight (≈ 1.4 vs 0.78), so the model pays more attention to the minority class. We compare it for RF and Logistic Regression.

Insight: class_weight="balanced" trades precision for recall:

  • RF: recall 0.673 → 0.723, precision 0.804 → 0.752, F1 +0.0044 (0.7324 → 0.7368);
  • Logistic Regression: recall 0.541 → 0.665, F1 +0.027 (0.6424 → 0.6694).

The price is many more false alarms: FPR rises from 9.0% to 13.0% (RF) and from 7.9% to 17.5% (LR). ROC-AUC barely moves (0.8736 → 0.8731), which shows class weighting mainly shifts the decision threshold. Because section 9 tunes the threshold explicitly, class weight is left to the RF search.

5. Random Forest tuning¶

  • RandomizedSearchCV with n_iter=25 random combinations of the search space below.
  • 3 grouped folds on a ~150k-row training subset made of whole domains (class ratio kept).
  • Scoring: F1, ROC-AUC, precision and recall. The best combination is the one with the best mean CV F1 (refit="f1").
  • n_jobs=1 inside each RF. The number of parallel search workers comes from the memory guard below: worst case of the space on one fold × workers ≤ free RAM − 1 GB.
  • The best parameters are then refit on the full training set.
In [12]:
idx150k = D.grouped_sample(train, 150_000, random_state=RS)
sub = train.iloc[idx150k].reset_index(drop=True)
cv3_sub = D.grouped_cv_splits(sub["registered_domain"], 3, RS)
print(f"tuning subset: {len(sub):,} rows from {sub.registered_domain.nunique():,} domains, "
      f"malicious {sub.label.mean():.3f}")
RF_SPACE = {"n_estimators": [100, 150, 200, 300, 400], "max_depth": [10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 40, None],
            "min_samples_split": [2, 5, 10, 20], "min_samples_leaf": [1, 2, 4, 8],
            "max_features": ["sqrt", "log2", 0.3, 0.5],
            "class_weight": [None, "balanced", "balanced_subsample"], "max_samples": [None, 0.5, 0.8]}
SCORING = ["f1", "roc_auc", "precision", "recall"]

def run_search(path, estimator, space, n_iter, n_jobs):
    if path.exists():
        return joblib.load(path)
    s = RandomizedSearchCV(estimator, space, n_iter=n_iter, scoring=SCORING, refit="f1", cv=cv3_sub,
                           n_jobs=n_jobs, random_state=RS, verbose=1)
    t = time.perf_counter(); s.fit(sub[FEATS], sub["label"].to_numpy()); dt = time.perf_counter() - t
    res = {"cv_results": pd.DataFrame(s.cv_results_), "best_params": s.best_params_,
           "best_score": float(s.best_score_), "time_s": dt, "n_iter": n_iter, "n_jobs": n_jobs, "rows": len(sub)}
    joblib.dump(res, path)
    return res

import psutil
# --- memory guard: worst case of the search space on ONE fold, times the workers, must fit in free RAM - 1 GB
mem_guard_path = ROOT / "reports/metrics/rf_search_memory_guard.json"
if (M.CACHE / "rf_search.joblib").exists() and mem_guard_path.exists():
    guard = json.loads(mem_guard_path.read_text())          # decision recorded in the real run
else:
    fold_rows = max(len(a) for a, _ in cv3_sub)
    worst_model_mb = bench["rf200_in_memory_mb"] * (max(RF_SPACE["n_estimators"]) / 200) * (fold_rows / bench["bench_rows"])
    worker_overhead_mb = 300.0      # python + sklearn + memmapped data per loky worker (measured 327 MB min in an aborted 8-worker run)
    per_worker_mb = worst_model_mb + worker_overhead_mb
    free_mb = psutil.virtual_memory().available / 1e6
    budget_mb = free_mb - 1000.0
    n_jobs_fit = int(max(1, min(os.cpu_count(), budget_mb // per_worker_mb)))
    guard = {"worst_case": "400 trees, max_depth None, min_samples_leaf 1, max_samples None",
             "fold_train_rows": int(fold_rows), "worst_model_mb": round(worst_model_mb), "worker_overhead_mb": worker_overhead_mb,
             "per_worker_worst_mb": round(per_worker_mb), "free_ram_mb_at_start": round(free_mb), "budget_mb (free - 1 GB)": round(budget_mb),
             "n_jobs_requested": -1, "n_jobs_used": n_jobs_fit, "worst_total_mb": round(n_jobs_fit * per_worker_mb)}
    mem_guard_path.write_text(json.dumps(guard, indent=2))
SEARCH_JOBS_RF = guard["n_jobs_used"]
display(pd.Series(guard, name="RF search memory guard").to_frame())
print(f"-> n_jobs reduced from -1 (24 cores) to {SEARCH_JOBS_RF} so the worst case "
      f"({guard['worst_total_mb']:,} MB) stays below free RAM - 1 GB ({guard['budget_mb (free - 1 GB)']:,} MB). Search space unchanged.")

rf_search = run_search(M.CACHE / "rf_search.joblib", RandomForestClassifier(n_jobs=1, random_state=RS),
                       RF_SPACE, N_ITER_RF, SEARCH_JOBS_RF)

def top_table(res, k=10):
    r = res["cv_results"].sort_values("rank_test_f1").head(k)
    pcols = [c for c in r.columns if c.startswith("param_")]
    t = r[pcols + ["mean_test_f1", "std_test_f1", "mean_test_roc_auc", "mean_test_precision",
                   "mean_test_recall", "mean_fit_time"]].copy()
    t.columns = [c.replace("param_", "") for c in t.columns]
    return t.reset_index(drop=True)

rf_top = top_table(rf_search)
M.save_metrics_table(rf_top, "rf_search_top10")
rf_top.round(4)

The top 10 are close together (CV F1 0.7181–0.7319), while the standard deviation across the 3 folds is 0.02–0.03. So the ranking among the top candidates is within fold-to-fold noise. All top-10 candidates use class_weight balanced or balanced_subsample, and 6 of the 10 use max_samples=0.8.

Insight: Mean CV F1 per parameter value (black line):

  • max_depth matters most. Depth 10 is clearly too shallow (≈ 0.690), depths 15–40 are best (≈ 0.717–0.722), and unlimited depth is slightly worse again (≈ 0.711). A moderate cap regularises the trees, which matches the large overfitting gap of the default RF in figure 15.
  • Fewer features per split work better on average. log2 and sqrt (≈ 0.726) beat 0.5 (≈ 0.704), although the single best candidate used 0.3.
  • min_samples_leaf has little effect (1–4 ≈ 0.715–0.718, 8 ≈ 0.710).

Deployability: ≤ 25 MB compressed and ≤ 20 ms single-URL latency¶

If the tuned RF is too big or too slow, we look for the smallest RF within 0.3 F1 points (0.003) of it. We keep its best settings and shrink it with fewer trees, a larger min_samples_leaf and a max_depth cap.

In [15]:
def deployable(key):
    m = store.meta(key)
    return m["size_mb"] <= LIM_MB and m["latency_ms_median"] <= LIM_MS

def val_f1(key, thr=0.5):
    return f1_score(yva, store.proba(key, "val") >= thr)

tuned_f1 = val_f1("rf_tuned")
# Overrides on top of the best parameters. Sized from the measured ~14 bytes per tree node after
# compression (default RF: 388 MB): <= 25 MB means roughly <= 1.8M nodes in the whole forest.
VARIANTS = [
    {"n_estimators": 100, "min_samples_leaf": 8},
    {"n_estimators": 100, "min_samples_leaf": 32},
    {"n_estimators": 100, "min_samples_leaf": 64},
    {"n_estimators": 100, "max_depth": 13},
    {"n_estimators": 100, "max_depth": 12},
    {"n_estimators": 100, "min_samples_leaf": 16, "max_depth": 13},
    {"n_estimators": 50, "min_samples_leaf": 16},
    {"n_estimators": 50, "min_samples_leaf": 32},
    {"n_estimators": 50, "max_depth": 12},
    {"n_estimators": 200, "max_depth": 10},
]
def variant_params(ov):
    """Best params + overrides, never LESS regularised than the tuned RF."""
    p = {**RF_BEST, **ov}
    p["min_samples_leaf"] = max(p["min_samples_leaf"], RF_BEST.get("min_samples_leaf", 1))
    p["n_estimators"] = min(p["n_estimators"], RF_BEST.get("n_estimators", 10**6))
    if RF_BEST.get("max_depth") is not None and p.get("max_depth") is not None:
        p["max_depth"] = min(p["max_depth"], RF_BEST["max_depth"])
    elif RF_BEST.get("max_depth") is not None:
        p["max_depth"] = RF_BEST["max_depth"]
    return p

rows = [{"key": "rf_tuned", **{k: RF_BEST.get(k) for k in ("n_estimators", "min_samples_leaf", "max_depth")}}]
if deployable("rf_tuned"):
    print("the tuned RF already meets both limits")
else:
    for i, ov in enumerate(VARIANTS):
        params = variant_params(ov)
        key = f"rf_small_{i}"
        store.ensure(key, "bagging", lambda p=params: RandomForestClassifier(**p, n_jobs=-1, random_state=RS),
                     Xtr, ytr, extra=M.rf_size_stats, note=json.dumps(ov))
        rows.append({"key": key, **{k: params.get(k) for k in ("n_estimators", "min_samples_leaf", "max_depth")}})
trade = pd.DataFrame(rows)
trade["val_f1"] = [val_f1(k) for k in trade.key]
trade["delta_f1_pts"] = 100 * (trade.val_f1 - tuned_f1)
trade["size_mb"] = [store.meta(k)["size_mb"] for k in trade.key]
trade["latency_ms"] = [store.meta(k)["latency_ms_median"] for k in trade.key]
trade["deployable"] = [deployable(k) for k in trade.key]
ok = trade[trade.deployable & (trade.delta_f1_pts >= -0.3)]
if len(ok):
    RF_DEPLOY = ok.sort_values("size_mb").iloc[0].key
    why = "smallest deployable RF within 0.3 F1 points of the tuned RF"
else:
    dep = trade[trade.deployable]
    RF_DEPLOY = dep.sort_values("val_f1", ascending=False).iloc[0].key if len(dep) else "rf_tuned"
    why = "no RF within 0.3 points met the limits -> best deployable RF"
RF_DEPLOY_PARAMS = variant_params(json.loads(store.meta(RF_DEPLOY)["note"])) if RF_DEPLOY != "rf_tuned" else dict(RF_BEST)
LABELS[RF_DEPLOY] = "Random Forest (tuned, deployable)"
M.save_metrics_table(trade.set_index("key"), "rf_size_vs_f1")
display(trade.round(4))
print(f"RF_DEPLOY = {RF_DEPLOY} ({why}); params = {RF_DEPLOY_PARAMS}")

Insight: We tried 10 smaller variants. rf_small_6 (50 trees, min_samples_leaf 16, depth 15) is the smallest RF within 0.3 F1 points of the tuned RF: 6.5 MB, 3.4 ms, F1 0.7424 (-0.19 points). More aggressive shrinking costs more: leaf 64 gives -3.3 points and depth 10 gives -4.1 points. Even the smallest variant (3.9 MB, 50 trees, depth 12) loses only 0.76 points. That means most of the 388 MB in the default RF was memorised noise.

6. Booster tuning¶

We tune whichever of XGBoost / LightGBM had the higher validation F1 in the baseline: n_iter=15, the same 3 grouped folds on the same 150k subset, n_jobs=1 inside the model and all cores for the search. Boosters are small in memory, so the search can use all cores.

In [17]:
BOOSTER = "xgboost" if val_f1("xgboost") >= val_f1("lightgbm") else "lightgbm"
OTHER = "lightgbm" if BOOSTER == "xgboost" else "xgboost"
print(f"baseline val F1: xgboost {val_f1('xgboost'):.4f} | lightgbm {val_f1('lightgbm'):.4f} -> tune {BOOSTER}")
common = {"learning_rate": [0.03, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2], "n_estimators": [200, 400, 600, 800],
          "subsample": [0.6, 0.8, 1.0], "colsample_bytree": [0.5, 0.7, 0.9, 1.0], "reg_lambda": [0.5, 1, 2, 5]}
if BOOSTER == "xgboost":
    B_EST = XGBClassifier(tree_method="hist", n_jobs=1, random_state=RS, eval_metric="logloss")
    B_SPACE = {**common, "max_depth": [4, 6, 8, 10, 12], "min_child_weight": [1, 3, 5, 10]}
else:
    B_EST = LGBMClassifier(n_jobs=1, random_state=RS, verbose=-1, subsample_freq=1)
    B_SPACE = {**common, "num_leaves": [31, 63, 127, 255], "min_child_samples": [10, 20, 50, 100]}
b_search = run_search(M.CACHE / f"{BOOSTER}_search.joblib", B_EST, B_SPACE, N_ITER_BOOST, -1)
B_BEST = dict(b_search["best_params"])
print(f"search: {b_search['n_iter']} x 3 folds in {b_search['time_s']/60:.1f} min; best CV F1 {b_search['best_score']:.4f}")
print("best parameters:", B_BEST)
B_TUNED = f"{BOOSTER}_tuned"

def make_booster_tuned():
    return clone(B_EST).set_params(**B_BEST, n_jobs=-1)

store.ensure(B_TUNED, "boosting", make_booster_tuned, Xtr, ytr, note="best search params refit on full train")

7. Voting & Stacking with the tuned members¶

Members: the deployable tuned RF, the tuned booster and the other booster with its baseline settings. We use the deployable RF because an ensemble containing the full-size RF could never meet the 25 MB limit.

In [18]:

    return RandomForestClassifier(**RF_DEPLOY_PARAMS, n_jobs=-1, random_state=RS)

8. Label-noise experiment¶

Step 1 documented label noise in the Kaggle data. We retrain the deployable tuned RF on the training split minus those rows (validation and test stay untouched), and we do not relabel anything:

  • Kaggle phishing-labelled pages on ietf.org (RFC documents) and wikipedia.org;
  • benign-labelled URLs containing webscr (PayPal's login script, a classic phishing-kit path).

Decision rule, fixed before looking at the results. The validation set contains the same kinds of noisy rows: a model that learned the noise is rewarded there. So the primary metric is validation F1 on the noise-free part of validation, each model at its own threshold (section 9 rule: best F1 with FPR ≤ 1%). If the difference is below 0.1 F1 points, it is a tie, broken first by fewer real-world false positives and then by higher OpenPhish recall. If it is still a tie, we keep the original (no rows removed).

In [19]:
def noise_mask(df):
    kaggle_phish = (df.source == "kaggle_malicious_phish") & (df.type == "phishing")
    ietf_wiki = kaggle_phish & df.registered_domain.isin(["ietf.org", "wikipedia.org"])
    webscr = (df.label == 0) & df.url_normalized.str.lower().str.contains("webscr", regex=False)
    return ietf_wiki, webscr

tr_iw, tr_ws = noise_mask(train); va_iw, va_ws = noise_mask(val)
tr_noise, va_noise = (tr_iw | tr_ws).to_numpy(), (va_iw | va_ws).to_numpy()
print(f"train noisy rows: {tr_noise.sum():,} (ietf/wikipedia 'phishing' {int(tr_iw.sum()):,}, 'benign' webscr {int(tr_ws.sum()):,})")
print(f"val   noisy rows: {va_noise.sum():,} (ietf/wikipedia 'phishing' {int(va_iw.sum()):,}, 'benign' webscr {int(va_ws.sum()):,})")
store.ensure(f"{RF_DEPLOY}_noiseclean", "bagging", rf_deploy_factory, Xtr[~tr_noise], ytr[~tr_noise],
             extra=M.rf_size_stats, note=f"trained without {int(tr_noise.sum())} documented noisy rows")
LABELS[f"{RF_DEPLOY}_noiseclean"] = "RF deployable, noise removed"

def eval_at_own_threshold(key):
    p = store.proba(key, "val")
    thr, _ = M.pick_threshold(yva, p)
    full = M.binary_metrics(yva, p, thr)
    nf = M.binary_metrics(yva[~va_noise], p[~va_noise], thr)
    noisy_pred_mal = float((p[va_noise] >= thr).mean()) if va_noise.any() else np.nan
    return {"threshold": thr, "val_f1": full["f1"], "val_precision": full["precision"], "val_recall": full["recall"],
            "val_fpr": full["fpr"], "val_roc_auc": full["roc_auc"], "noise_free_val_f1": nf["f1"],
            "noise_free_val_fpr": nf["fpr"], "noisy_val_rows_predicted_malicious": noisy_pred_mal,
            "realworld_fp": int((store.proba(key, "realworld") >= thr).sum()),
            "openphish_recall": float((store.proba(key, "openphish") >= thr).mean())}

ln = pd.DataFrame({"original train": eval_at_own_threshold(RF_DEPLOY),
                   "noisy rows removed": eval_at_own_threshold(f"{RF_DEPLOY}_noiseclean")}).T
M.save_metrics_table(ln, "label_noise_experiment")
a, b = ln.loc["original train"], ln.loc["noisy rows removed"]
diff = 100 * (b.noise_free_val_f1 - a.noise_free_val_f1)
if diff >= 0.1:
    ADOPT_CLEAN, reason = True, f"noise-free val F1 +{diff:.2f} pts"
elif diff <= -0.1:
    ADOPT_CLEAN, reason = False, f"noise-free val F1 {diff:.2f} pts"
elif b.realworld_fp != a.realworld_fp:
    ADOPT_CLEAN, reason = b.realworld_fp < a.realworld_fp, f"tie on F1 ({diff:+.2f} pts) -> real-world FP {a.realworld_fp:.0f} vs {b.realworld_fp:.0f}"
elif b.openphish_recall != a.openphish_recall:
    ADOPT_CLEAN, reason = b.openphish_recall > a.openphish_recall, f"tie -> OpenPhish recall {a.openphish_recall:.3f} vs {b.openphish_recall:.3f}"
else:
    ADOPT_CLEAN, reason = False, "complete tie -> keep original"
display(ln.T.round(4))
print(f"DECISION: {'TRAIN WITHOUT the noisy rows' if ADOPT_CLEAN else 'KEEP the original training data'} ({reason})")

Insight: We removed 7,897 noisy training rows: 3,760 Kaggle phishing-labelled ietf.org/wikipedia.org pages and 4,137 benign-labelled webscr URLs. Validation contains 775 noisy rows (all webscr) and 0 ietf/wikipedia rows, because those domains fell into train and test.

Results for the deployable RF at its own FPR ≤ 1% threshold:

  • noise-free validation F1 rose from 0.5361 to 0.5503 (+1.41 points), with recall +1.4 points and precision unchanged at 0.956;
  • real-world false positives stayed at 0;
  • OpenPhish recall dropped slightly (76.5% → 75.8%, 2 URLs).

By the rule fixed in advance, we train the final candidates without the noisy rows. Nothing was relabelled.

In [20]:
# Apply the decision to the final candidates (RF, tuned booster, tuned ensembles).
SUFFIX = "_noiseclean" if ADOPT_CLEAN else ""
if ADOPT_CLEAN:
    Xc, yc = Xtr[~tr_noise], ytr[~tr_noise]
    cv3_clean = D.grouped_cv_splits(train.loc[~tr_noise, "registered_domain"], 3, RS)
    store.ensure(f"{B_TUNED}_noiseclean", "boosting", make_booster_tuned, Xc, yc)
    store.ensure(f"{OTHER}_noiseclean", "boosting", other_factory, Xc, yc)
    if not store.has("voting_tuned_noiseclean"):
        mem = [f"{RF_DEPLOY}_noiseclean", f"{B_TUNED}_noiseclean", f"{OTHER}_noiseclean"]
        vote = M.SoftVotingPrefit([store.load(n) for n in mem], mem)
        store.ensure("voting_tuned_noiseclean", "combination", None, None, None, fitted=vote,
                     fit_time_s=sum(store.meta(n)["fit_time_s"] for n in mem), note="members: " + ", ".join(mem))
        del vote; gc.collect()
    b1c, b2c = (make_booster_tuned(), other_factory()) if BOOSTER == "xgboost" else (other_factory(), make_booster_tuned())
    stack_c = StackingClassifier(estimators=[("rf", rf_deploy_factory()), ("xgb", b1c), ("lgbm", b2c)],
                                 final_estimator=LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000, random_state=RS),
                                 cv=cv3_clean, stack_method="predict_proba", n_jobs=1)
    store.ensure("stacking_tuned_noiseclean", "combination", lambda: stack_c, Xc, yc, post_fit=drop_cv)
    for k in [f"{B_TUNED}_noiseclean", f"{OTHER}_noiseclean", "voting_tuned_noiseclean", "stacking_tuned_noiseclean"]:
        LABELS[k] = LABELS.get(k.replace("_noiseclean", ""), k) + " [noise removed]"
FINAL_FAMILY = [RF_DEPLOY + SUFFIX, B_TUNED + SUFFIX, "voting_tuned" + SUFFIX, "stacking_tuned" + SUFFIX]
print("final tuned candidates:", FINAL_FAMILY)

9. Decision threshold¶

A probability of 0.5 is not automatically the best cut-off. For a browser extension, false alarms on normal sites are what make users uninstall it, so for every candidate we pick, on validation, the threshold that maximises F1 subject to FPR ≤ 1.0%.

In [21]:
ALL_KEYS = list(dict.fromkeys(BASE_KEYS + ["rf_balanced", "logreg_balanced", "rf_tuned"] +
                              [k for k in trade.key if k != "rf_tuned"] + [B_TUNED, "voting_tuned", "stacking_tuned",
                              f"{RF_DEPLOY}_noiseclean"] + FINAL_FAMILY))
ALL_KEYS = [k for k in ALL_KEYS if store.has(k)]
SUPERSEDED = [RF_DEPLOY, B_TUNED, "voting_tuned", "stacking_tuned"] if ADOPT_CLEAN else []
CANDS = [k for k in ALL_KEYS if deployable(k) and k not in SUPERSEDED]
no_fpr = [k for k in CANDS if M.binary_metrics(yva, store.proba(k, "val"), M.pick_threshold(yva, store.proba(k, "val"))[0])["fpr"] > 0.01]
CANDS = [k for k in CANDS if k not in no_fpr]
print("superseded by their noise-removed retrain (not candidates):", SUPERSEDED)
print("cannot reach FPR <= 1% at any threshold (not candidates):", no_fpr)

for k in CANDS:

    rows.append({"model": LABELS.get(k, k), "key": k, "threshold": thr, "f1@thr": mt["f1"], "precision@thr": mt["precision"],
                 "recall@thr": mt["recall"], "fpr@thr": mt["fpr"], "f1@0.5": m05["f1"], "fpr@0.5": m05["fpr"],
                 "realworld_fp": int((store.proba(k, "realworld") >= thr).sum()),
                 "openphish_recall": float((store.proba(k, "openphish") >= thr).mean()),
                 "size_mb": store.meta(k)["size_mb"], "latency_ms": store.meta(k)["latency_ms_median"],
                 "contains_rf": ("rf" in k) or ("random_forest" in k) or k.startswith(("voting", "stacking"))})

16 Logistic Regression 0.83 0.4560 0.9462 0.3004 0.0093 0.6424 0.0785 0 0.7081 0.003 1.2917 False
17 Logistic Regression (balanced) 0.90 0.4526 0.9440 0.2977 0.0096 0.6694 0.1749 0 0.6946 0.003 1.6067 False
18 AdaBoost (stumps) 0.56 0.3985 0.9523 0.2520 0.0069 0.6065 0.0930 0 0.7584 0.027 17.2227 False

Insight: The limits exclude several models:

  • 7 models are too big or too slow (the full-depth forests, the full tuned RF and the default-RF ensembles);
  • 3 can never reach FPR ≤ 1% (Decision Tree, KNN, Naive Bayes);
  • 4 tuned models were replaced by their noise-removed retrains.

That leaves 19 real candidates. Holding FPR at or below 1% forces high thresholds (0.80–0.90). Precision rises to about 0.96, but recall falls to 0.25–0.49, so F1 at these thresholds is 0.40–0.65 instead of 0.70–0.75 at 0.5.

The best candidate is XGBoost (tuned, noise removed): F1 0.6542 at 0.80, with 9 real-world false positives. Soft Voting (noise removed) follows at 0.6469 with 5 false positives. All the deployable RF variants land at F1 0.52–0.55, but with 0–1 real-world false positives.

Insight: Each panel shows the trade-off. F1 peaks near the middle thresholds, but there FPR is 7–14%: a user would see a false alarm on roughly 1 in 10 normal pages. Moving right until FPR (yellow line, ×10) falls below the 1% line costs recall (orange), while precision (blue) approaches 1. F1 peaks at about 0.75 around thresholds 0.35–0.5 and falls to about 0.55–0.65 at the chosen 0.80–0.84.

10. Model selection¶

Rule (applied exactly as specified):

  1. Candidates = models that meet the deployability limits (≤ 25 MB, ≤ 20 ms).
  2. Best = the candidate with the highest validation F1 at its own threshold.
  3. Deploy the tuned RF (its deployable version) if it is within 1.0 F1 point of the best.
  4. Otherwise deploy the best candidate, preferring an ensemble that contains RF when one is within 1.0 point of the best.
  5. Tie-breakers: fewer real-world false positives, then higher OpenPhish recall.
In [23]:
RF_FINAL = RF_DEPLOY + SUFFIX
ranked = cand.copy()
ranked["f1_pts"] = (100 * ranked["f1@thr"]).round(2)
ranked = ranked.sort_values(["f1_pts", "realworld_fp", "openphish_recall"], ascending=[False, True, False]).reset_index(drop=True)
best = ranked.iloc[0]
rf_row = ranked[ranked.key == RF_FINAL]
if len(rf_row) and (best["f1@thr"] - rf_row.iloc[0]["f1@thr"]) * 100 <= 1.0:
    SELECTED, rule = RF_FINAL, (f"tuned RF is within 1.0 F1 point of the best candidate "
                                f"({100*rf_row.iloc[0]['f1@thr']:.2f} vs {100*best['f1@thr']:.2f})")
else:
    near = ranked[(best["f1@thr"] - ranked["f1@thr"]) * 100 <= 1.0]
    ens = near[near.key.str.startswith(("voting", "stacking"))]
    if len(ens):
        SELECTED, rule = ens.iloc[0].key, "tuned RF not within 1.0 point -> RF-containing ensemble within 1.0 point of the best"
    else:
        SELECTED, rule = best.key, "tuned RF not within 1.0 point -> best candidate"
sel = ranked[ranked.key == SELECTED].iloc[0]
THRESHOLD = float(sel.threshold)

Decision: deploy Soft Voting (tuned members) [noise removed] (voting_tuned_noiseclean) at threshold 0.80¶

Reason: tuned RF not within 1.0 point -> RF-containing ensemble within 1.0 point of the best. Best candidate by F1: XGBoost (tuned) [noise removed] (65.42). Selected: F1 64.69, FPR 0.97%, 13.3 MB, 14.1 ms.

Insight: Applying the rule:

  1. The best candidate is XGBoost (tuned, noise removed) at 65.42 F1 points.
  2. The deployable tuned RF (noise removed) reaches 55.02, which is 10.4 points behind, so it does not qualify under the 1-point rule.
  3. Among candidates within 1.0 point of the best, the rule prefers an ensemble that contains RF. Soft Voting (tuned RF + tuned XGBoost + LightGBM, noise removed) scores 64.69, which is 0.73 points behind.

So we deploy Soft Voting at threshold 0.80: 13.3 MB, 14.1 ms, 5 real-world false positives (vs 9 for XGBoost alone) and 79.2% OpenPhish recall.

11. Final test evaluation: the test set is used once, here¶

Only the selected model (at its validation-chosen threshold) and the tuned RF (for reference, at its own validation threshold) are scored on the test set.

Insight: On the untouched test set (132,632 URLs from domains never used before), the selected Soft Voting at threshold 0.80 scores:

  • precision 0.9657, recall 0.4616, F1 0.6246;
  • FPR 0.84%, so the false-alarm target holds on new data;
  • ROC-AUC 0.8883, PR-AUC 0.8478.

These are close to the validation numbers (F1 0.6469), so the threshold was not overfitted to validation. The tuned full-size RF scores F1 0.5499 at its own threshold.

In plain words: when the model raises an alarm it is right 97% of the time, but it lets through about half of the malicious URLs it has never seen anything like.

  • malware 84.6%: IP:port downloads and executable files are easy to recognise;
  • defacement 64.5%: Joomla-style query strings;
  • phishing only 31.9%: phishing URLs increasingly look like ordinary URLs.

Benign FPR is 0.84%. By source, the model does better on PhiUSIIL (F1 0.6542, FPR 0.19%) than on Kaggle (F1 0.6106, FPR 1.04%), whose labels are noisier.

12. OpenPhish fresh test¶

These are live phishing URLs captured on 2026-11-24, years after most of the training data, so this is the closest thing we have to "what the extension will meet tomorrow".

def op_pattern(row):
    h, u = row["host"], row["url_normalized"].lower()
    if "ipfs" in u: return "IPFS gateway"
    if any(s in h for s in ("sites.google.com", "docs.google.com", "forms.gle", "forms.office.com", "storage.googleapis.com")) or "google.com/forms" in u:
        return "Google Sites / Forms / Storage"
    if re.search(FREE_HOSTING, h): return "free hosting / site builder"
    if F.is_ip_host(h): return "IP-address host"
    if F.parse_url(h).registered_domain in F.SHORTENERS: return "URL shortener"
    return "own domain"

Insight: On live phishing collected in November 2026, recall is 79.2% (236/298). That is far above the test recall, because 243 URLs are on free hosting / site builders, where recall is 92.6% (mostly *.pages.dev, a platform already seen in training).

On the 50 never-seen domains, recall is only 22.0% (11/50), and for phishing on its own domain 20.4%. That is the honest weak spot. Many misses are plain-looking hosts (complianceguides.org, inboxmailapp.com), look-alikes (sh0pify15.com, roblox.com.pt) and brand-new domains. Nothing in their URL text separates them from a small legitimate site.

ax.axvline(THRESHOLD, color=V.INK, lw=1.2); ax.text(THRESHOLD, ax.get_ylim()[1] * 0.92, f" threshold {THRESHOLD:.2f}", fontsize=9)
ax.set_xlabel("P(malicious) from the selected model"); ax.set_ylabel("URLs"); ax.legend(loc="upper center")
ax.set_title("Fresh phishing vs real-world benign URLs: predicted probability")
fig.tight_layout(); V.savefig(fig, 23, "openphish_vs_realworld_probability"); plt.show()

Insight: 5 of the 86 legitimate URLs (5.8%) are flagged at threshold 0.80 (26 at 0.5):

  • a Google Form (0.834) and a Google Slides link (0.825);
  • the login pages of GitHub (0.824), PayPal (0.823) and Netflix (0.818).

All of them are short URLs with a login keyword, or long random document IDs: exactly what phishing URLs look like. The bank, government, education, Wikipedia and StackOverflow URLs all stay below 0.70. This is why the API adds a curated trusted-domain list. It covers github.com, paypal.com, netflix.com and docs.google.com documents, but deliberately not Google Forms, which anyone can create. The notebook metrics stay model-only.

14. Feature importance¶

  • Impurity importance (Random Forest's built-in value): how much each feature reduced Gini impurity across all splits. It is fast, but biased towards features with many distinct values.
  • Permutation importance (model-agnostic): how much the selected model's ROC-AUC drops when one feature's values are shuffled. Computed on a 20k validation sample with n_repeats=5.
In [30]:
from sklearn.inspection import permutation_importance
imp_path = M.CACHE / f"importance_{SELECTED}.joblib"
if imp_path.exists():
    IMP = joblib.load(imp_path)
else:
    rf_model = store.load(RF_FINAL)
    impurity = pd.Series(rf_model.feature_importances_, index=FEATS)
    del rf_model; gc.collect()
    sel_model = M.set_n_jobs(store.load(SELECTED), -1)
    si = val.sample(20_000, random_state=RS).index
    t = time.perf_counter()
    pi = permutation_importance(sel_model, Xva.loc[si], yva[val.index.get_indexer(si)], scoring="roc_auc",
                                n_repeats=5, random_state=RS, n_jobs=1)
    IMP = {"impurity": impurity, "perm_mean": pd.Series(pi.importances_mean, index=FEATS),
           "perm_std": pd.Series(pi.importances_std, index=FEATS), "time_s": time.perf_counter() - t}
    joblib.dump(IMP, imp_path); del sel_model; gc.collect()
imp = pd.DataFrame({"impurity (RF)": IMP["impurity"], "permutation ΔROC-AUC (selected)": IMP["perm_mean"],
                    "perm std": IMP["perm_std"]})
imp["rank impurity"] = imp["impurity (RF)"].rank(ascending=False).astype(int)
imp["rank permutation"] = imp["permutation ΔROC-AUC (selected)"].rank(ascending=False).astype(int)
from scipy.stats import spearmanr
rho = spearmanr(imp["impurity (RF)"], imp["permutation ΔROC-AUC (selected)"]).statistic
M.save_metrics_table(imp.sort_values("rank permutation"), "feature_importance")
print(f"permutation importance took {IMP['time_s']:.0f}s; Spearman rank correlation impurity vs permutation = {rho:.2f}")
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 6.5))
for ax, col, title in [(axes[0], "impurity (RF)", f"RF impurity importance (top 20)"),
                       (axes[1], "permutation ΔROC-AUC (selected)", f"Permutation importance, selected model (top 20)")]:
    s = imp[col].sort_values().tail(20)
    ax.barh(s.index, s.values, color=V.FAMILY_COLORS["bagging"] if ax is axes[0] else V.SERIES_COLORS[0], height=0.7)
    if ax is axes[1]:
        ax.errorbar(s.values, range(len(s)), xerr=imp.loc[s.index, "perm std"], fmt="none", ecolor=V.INK_2, lw=1)
    ax.set_title(title)
fig.tight_layout(); V.savefig(fig, 24, "feature_importance_impurity_vs_permutation"); plt.show()
imp.sort_values("rank permutation").head(20).round(4)

Insight: Both methods agree on the leader: tld_malicious_rate (impurity 0.229, permutation ΔROC-AUC 0.070, more than 3× the next feature). After that come structure features: path_len, num_dots, tld_len and host_num_digits. The rank correlation between the two methods is 0.79.

Where they disagree, permutation importance is the more trustworthy one. risky_file_extension and num_query_params rank much higher by permutation (6th and 4th) than by impurity (28th and 17th): they are rare or low-cardinality, and impurity importance is biased against such features.

15. Error analysis (test set, selected model)¶

Below are the 20 most confident false positives and the 20 most confident false negatives, each with an automatic pattern note. We then count how many of all test errors match the label-noise patterns documented in Step 1.

In [31]:
te_iw, te_ws = noise_mask(test)
def note(row):
    u, h = row.url_normalized.lower(), str(row.registered_domain)
    if "webscr" in u and row.label == 0: return "label noise: PayPal kit path labelled benign"
    if row.label == 1 and h in ("ietf.org", "wikipedia.org"): return "label noise: ietf/wikipedia labelled phishing"
    if "option=com_" in u or "index.php?" in u: return "CMS / Joomla-style query"
    if F.is_ip_host(F.parse_url(row.url_normalized).host): return "IP-address host"
    if re.search(FREE_HOSTING, u): return "free hosting / site builder"
    if "/" not in row.url_normalized and "?" not in row.url_normalized: return "bare domain, no path"
    if len(u) > 120: return "very long URL"
    return "other"
test["proba"] = p_sel; test["pred"] = pred_sel
fp_te = test[(test.label == 0) & (test.pred == 1)].sort_values("proba", ascending=False)
fn_te = test[(test.label == 1) & (test.pred == 0)].sort_values("proba")
for name, d in [("false positives", fp_te), ("false negatives", fn_te)]:
    top = d.head(20).copy(); top["note"] = top.apply(note, axis=1)
    print(f"{name}: {len(d):,} in total; the 20 most confident:")
    display(top[["url_original", "type", "source", "proba", "note"]].round(3))
errs = pd.concat([fp_te, fn_te]); errs["note"] = errs.apply(note, axis=1)
err_tab = errs.groupby(["label", "note"]).size().unstack(0, fill_value=0).rename(columns={0: "false positives", 1: "false negatives"})
err_tab["total"] = err_tab.sum(axis=1)
noise_err = int(errs.note.str.startswith("label noise").sum())
print(f"test errors: {len(errs):,}; matching documented label-noise patterns: {noise_err:,} ({100*noise_err/len(errs):.2f}%)")
# Beyond the Step 1 patterns: well-known content sites among the most confident false negatives
known_content = errs[(errs.label == 1) & errs.registered_domain.isin(["springer.com", "eweek.com", "dailykos.com", "linenghb.com"])]
print(f"false negatives on springer.com / eweek.com / dailykos.com / linenghb.com (likely mislabelled content pages): {len(known_content):,}")
print(f"(test rows matching the noise patterns: {int((te_iw | te_ws).sum()):,})")
M.save_metrics_table(err_tab, "test_error_patterns")
err_tab.sort_values("total", ascending=False)

Insight: The 738 false positives are dominated by two patterns:

  • Joomla-style CMS pages labelled benign (index.php?option=com_content...), the overlap with defacement we predicted in Step 1;
  • bare PhiUSIIL homepages on high-risk TLDs (gouvernement.ga, starship.xyz, maslo.top).

The 24,263 false negatives are mostly normal-looking URLs. Among the most confident ones are 82 Kaggle phishing/malware rows on springer.com, eweek.com, dailykos.com and linenghb.com that look like ordinary article or product pages: more label noise of the ietf.org kind, which Step 1 had not documented. Only 11 test errors (0.04%) match the Step 1 noise patterns, because those domains are concentrated in train (the grouped split).

Insight: * Model: the deployed model is Soft Voting of a tuned 50-tree Random Forest, tuned XGBoost and LightGBM, trained without the documented noisy rows, at threshold 0.80.

  • Test set: precision 0.966, recall 0.462, F1 0.625, FPR 0.84%, ROC-AUC 0.888.
  • OpenPhish: recall 79.2% overall, but 22.0% on never-seen domains.
  • Real-world: 5/86 false positives, handled in the API by the trusted list.
  • Footprint: 13.3 MB, 14.1 ms per URL, 247 MB RSS.

Limitations to present honestly:

  1. URL-only features cannot recognise phishing on brand-new, plain-looking domains.
  2. Holding false alarms at 1% halves recall.
  3. The Kaggle labels contain more noise than documented.
